look_here_first: LOOK FOR THE SKINNY OFTEN INTERRUPTED SPIKE-LIKE HEAD: many spikelets, especially on upper branches, have NO obvious bristle; at most one SHORT bristle, often ≤2 mm, may occur below a spikelet. Then inspect slender leaves, hairs around the collar, and perennial knotty/hairy basal rhizomes. This is NOT a densely bristly foxtail.

best_field_traits: Texas perennial often forming a small to moderate upright tuft from shallow, hard, branched rhizomatous bases.
Fine basal blades; narrower stem blades often only a few mm wide.
Loose/slender, often broken or interrupted spike-like panicle, in local treatment about 5–15 cm long.
Bristles very sparse: upper solitary spikelets often bristleless; other branches may have one very short bristle, commonly ≤2 mm.
Spotted purplish 3–3.6 mm spikelets in local flora treatment; observe mature structures before claiming exact ID.
True ligule can form a hair curtain around 1–2 mm; hairs in the leaf collar can be longer and must not be mistaken for the ligule.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole tuft with slender flowering heads in daylight
Head macro showing *bristleless* upper spikelets and any isolated short bristles
Leaf blade and sheath with width scale
Separate true ligule vs longer collar hairs, side-by-side and measured
Base/rhizome attachment with stem plus mature 3-mm spikelets
crew_field_check: Count bristles under 10× magnification; these are reduced branches, NOT true awns.
Measure whole flowering head and a mature spikelet.
Inspect the base/collar/rhizomes on the SAME PLANT; do not force identification from a single image.

comparisons.key_distinctions: S. parviflora has densely packed short foxtail heads with several bristles (often 6–7) below each spikelet, not the sparse short bristles here. S. scheelei has a denser, longer bottlebrush flowering head with a conspicuous long bristle beneath many spikelets. Cultivated S. italica has heavy densely seeded heads and broad leaves; not a native species.
